sections.summary: The neutral reading finds that Paul instructs a congregation described as biting and envying one another to mend anyone caught in a trespass, warns the mender in the singular that he stands in the same exposure, and sets shared crushing weight (baros) beside each person's own assigned load (phortion).
sections.relevance: The instruction presupposes that a member of a Spirit-possessing congregation can genuinely fall -- paraptoma, a slip off the path -- and that the one restoring him is equally liable to be overtaken ("lest you too be tempted"), which rules out any presumed invulnerability among "you who are spiritual." The reading also notes that the future "will bear his own load" may be a general future or may look toward a final accounting, a possibility the sowing-and-reaping material that follows immediately strengthens. The section addresses community practice rather than standing before God directly, so its bearing is real but indirect: it assumes real falling, real exposure, and individual answerability for one's own work.
key_phrases: if anyone is caught in any trespass
restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness
watch yourself, lest you too be tempted
let each one test his own work
each will bear his own load

sections.summary: The neutral reading finds that Paul restates the flesh-Spirit contrast agriculturally, using the proverbial sowing-and-reaping pattern whose two components are correspondence and delay: what is sown determines the crop, the crop comes in its own season, and it comes "if we do not give out."
sections.relevance: The reading presses two features directly onto this question. First, both harvests -- corruption from the flesh, eternal life from the Spirit -- use the same verb in the same tense and both follow from what was sown, so "eternal life is stated here as a crop reaped, which is to say as something arrived at rather than something held from the beginning and merely retained." Second, "the conditional is explicit and Paul does not soften it": the harvest arrives in its season if we do not give up (me eklyomenoi), and the sentence is built as a promise with a condition attached, both halves stated. The reading further sets this beside 5:4 and 5:21 as the third of three warnings of a single shape -- a connection severed, an inheritance not entered, a harvest not brought in -- and observes that none of them describes a possession confiscated. The "do not be deceived" formula signals that Paul is correcting something people are inclined to think, and "God is not mocked" states that the arrangement cannot be gamed by appearance. This is Paul's own argument in his own voice, addressed to believers in the first person plural, and it makes the eschatological outcome follow from ongoing conduct.
key_phrases: do not be deceived: God is not mocked
whatever a man sows, that he will also reap
the one who sows to his own flesh will from the flesh reap corruption
the one who sows to the Spirit will from the Spirit reap eternal life
in due season we will reap, if we do not give up
let us not grow weary in doing good

sections.section_title: The Postscript in Paul's Own Hand
sections.summary: The neutral reading finds that Paul takes the pen himself and restates four things -- the other teachers' motive, boasting, the cross, and new creation -- ruling out both circumcision and uncircumcision as counting for anything, blessing those who walk by that rule, producing his own scars as the counter-mark to circumcision, and closing with grace and the word "brothers."
sections.relevance: The postscript bears on the question through what it presupposes rather than through any statement about permanence. The compulsion to be circumcised is still being applied and has not yet succeeded (the reading notes the circumcision has not happened at 5:2 and the desertion is in progress at 1:6), so the letter's own summary assumes the readers stand at a decision whose outcome is not fixed -- and by the letter's terms at 5:4 that outcome carries severance from Christ and falling from grace. The reading also observes that the benediction wishes them charis, "the thing it warned them they were leaving," and that the whole severity is aimed at a movement the writer believes can still be reversed. Against this, the reading stresses that nothing in six chapters withdraws the address "brothers" and that the relationship the letter is written from does not change from first line to last, which cuts the other way. The section does not directly argue either position, so it leans rather than settles.
key_phrases: they would compel you to be circumcised
that they may boast in your flesh
the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world
neither circumcision counts for anything, nor uncircumcision, but a new creation
all who walk by this rule
the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit, brothers
